summary: Describes the routing requirements placed on the GMPLS protocol suite so that it can support the capabilities of an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) as defined by the ITU-T. It covers time-division connections such as SONET and SDH and optical transport networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4258 describes routing requirements for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) in the Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) architecture. It covers network areas, controllers, destinations that can be reached, and information about nodes and links.

what does gmpls routing need for ason
subtitle: Routing requirements for using GMPLS in the ASON optical-network control architecture.

tldr.problem: The ITU-T ASON control-plane architecture needs routing functions for optical and time-division networks. The IETF needed to record the routing requirements relevant to the GMPLS protocol suite.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes nested Routing Areas, protocol-independent Routing Controllers, exchange of reachability information, and common node and link attributes.
tldr.outcome: It is a conceptual requirements document. It does not assess GMPLS applicability or define a routing protocol or extension.

facts.label: Connection continuity
facts.value: Established calls must not be disrupted by controller failure

today: RFC 4258 is an Informational requirements document published in November 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it, and the document defines no routing protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Network Assumptions
sections.content:
GMPLS can control several switching technologies, including time-division connections over SONET or SDH and Optical Transport Networks. RFC 4258 summarizes routing requirements for supporting the ITU-T ASON control-plane architecture.

The document is protocol-neutral in its description. It does not decide whether GMPLS applies to ASON and does not propose a protocol design or extension. Operators choose how to divide a network into Routing Areas and which routing protocols to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists routing requirements for a system that controls optical networks. It does not select a routing method or tell operators how to divide their networks.

sections.title: Routing Areas and Controllers
sections.content:
A Routing Area (RA) is a network partition used to organize routing information. Areas may be nested, with child areas contained in parent areas. A Routing Controller (RC) handles routing information for an area and may be distributed across several entities; Link Resource Managers supply topology information, and RCs store it in a Routing Information Database.

Each area needs an identifier, and each controller identifier must be unique within its area. Before controllers communicate, they must verify that they share the same parent area. Failure of a controller or communication between controllers must not disrupt connections that are already established, although setup of new calls may be unavailable during recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can be divided into nested areas for sharing route information. Each area has a controller, and a controller failure must not interrupt connections already in progress.

sections.title: Exchanging and Updating Routing Information
sections.content:
Routing information may be exchanged between controllers in parent and child areas. It should include reachability and may include node or link topology, subject to policy. Controllers in sibling areas do not communicate directly under this model.

When information moves between levels, the protocol must prevent it from being reintroduced where it originated, which would create a loop. The RFC also calls for consistent information after filtering or summarizing and support for operator-assisted changes to the area hierarchy.
sections.plainLanguage: Larger and smaller network areas can share information about which destinations can be reached. The system must track where information came from so it does not circulate back to its source.

sections.title: Node and Link Information
sections.content:
The RFC groups routing attributes by whether they describe a node or link, whether they are configured or negotiated, and whether they are inherited from another network layer. The ASON control plane represents transport resources with Subnetwork Points and groups them into Subnetwork Point Pools for routing; this control-plane view need not match the physical topology.

Node ID is required as both a supported capability and operator-controlled information. Reachability is required as a capability. Link information includes local and remote link identifiers; listed characteristics include signal type, link weight, resource class, connection types and capacity, with availability, diversity and adaptation support also described.
sections.plainLanguage: Route messages describe network points, links and reachable destinations. The map used to control the network can group resources differently from the physical network.

sections.title: Security and Architectural Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC says the ASON routing protocol must meet applicable operational security objectives. A threat analysis should consider impersonation, eavesdropping, unauthorized access, loss or corruption of information, replay, forgery and denial of service. It notes that some security objectives may be met by other established means.

The architecture also requires unique area identifiers, support for multiple links, convergence of distributed routing databases, and the ability for a subnetwork or area to appear as one logical entity with only its external links visible outside.
sections.plainLanguage: The design must consider attacks that fake, expose, change or block route information. A smaller network should also be able to appear as one unit to the wider network.
